references.text: The Lord commands Moses to stretch out his hand, following the same pattern as in other plagues where Moses stretches out his hand or staff over Egypt.
Moses is commanded to stretch out his hand over Egypt, a formulation similar to that used in the locust plague.
Moses stretches out his hand toward heaven to bring hail upon Egypt, which destroyed much of the vegetation that the locusts would later consume.
A prior warning about the locust plague is now being carried out, where the locusts will devour what remains after the hail.
The fulfillment of the command in verse 12, as the locusts arrive and consume all the vegetation left by the hail.
Locusts are mentioned as an edible insect in the Mosaic Law, using the same Hebrew word (אַרְבֶּה).
Locusts that destroy crops are cited as a curse for disobedience, paralleling the plague upon Egypt.
The psalmist recalls how God gave Egypt's crops to the locusts as part of the plagues.
A poetic retelling of the locust plague where the locusts came and devoured all vegetation in the land.
Joel describes a locust plague that consumes all vegetation, similar to the Egyptian plague.
The Lord promises to restore what the locusts have consumed, referencing destruction like that in Egypt.
In Revelation, locusts rise from the abyss as a plague, with clear allusions to the locust plague in Egypt.
Both verses demonstrate God's sovereign control over nature through Moses' hand gestures to escalate judgment against Egypt's fertility.
The connection shows how the same prophetic action (stretching out the hand) both initiates the plagues against Egypt's resources and completes the judgment upon Egypt's military power.
Both verses in the same chapter show how Moses' gesture toward heaven triggers two complementary judgments (darkness and locusts) that strike at the foundation of Egypt's existence.
The verses illuminate the causality in God's plan: the locust plague is the decisive means that leads to the final exodus predicted in chapter 11.
